paragraphs.text: II. A Tract against Those Who Have Presumed to Write against the Synod
PREFACE.

The urge to speak is usually driven by a burning concern for one of several things. Either the mind is greedy for praise and wants to buy favour with its sweat, so that, amid the flatteries of glory, it ignores the torment of the one who speaks. Or, bound by the fetters of gain, it sells the service of its tongue, so that the mind, enslaved by the lust for possession, reckons it already holds the profit it expects, and so does not know how to fear the dangers that the exercise of the pen brings upon it. Or, hemmed in by necessity, it brings out speech that is captive and unpolished by any file, and openly shows a brow that knows no shame, so that, while it serves its purpose, it renounces all care for elegance. For the ornaments of speech belong not to business but to repose; painted words are not for warfare but for leisure. The battlefield demands a strong man, deep peace a man in garlands; whoever asserts what will do good despises language coloured with the brush of art. This being so, I set out the reason for my account, and I commend to devout minds a voice forced out of me by the barking of the wicked. I remember that it is written: A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. Or, after the warrant of the prophetic oracle, there is the example of a certain orator, who says that speaking is quite out of place except when it is necessary. So I devote the service of my mouth, as far as the strength of my talent allows, to the bishops, against whom the venom of hissing tongues has been poured out. Yet devout patience, protected by the shield of faith, does not fear the rain of darts, and weapons hurled without the skill of war return upon the one who threw them. For those whose breastplate is Christ do not fear violence, and they lay their enemies low by patient waiting. Yet would anyone think a battle in this line is something to dread, when the fight is waged against God and the bishops without any reckoning of strength? Would anyone see an enemy who wavers even while he provokes, and be terrified of an adversary whose grounds for war are so weak? A man begrudges himself the victory if he holds back from attacking an enemy already wounded by his own conscience. Whoever in a conflict weighs anything else before the causes is working for his enemy's gain. Innocence gives strength to javelins, and the will to fight, when it springs from justice, sharpens the blade; we know that righteous indignation has given force to a blow more than arms have. That is why a multitude has failed to withstand the weapons of a few. So, with the prophet saying with me, More are with us than with them, I shall begin a work that will, I think, please the good.

It would indeed be enough that schismatic ignorance has fallen by its own proposition, especially since the charges carry their own answer with them, and the title deserves to be condemned together with its author without any examination by reading. For the very heading makes known what this filthy work means when it says: AGAINST THE SYNOD OF THE UNFITTING ABSOLUTION. Yet I will now proceed as though one who puts forward evil needed to perish by someone else's sword. Can this preamble, most insane of men, be put down to mere ignorance? Is there anyone besides you who must be counted among the ulcerous and straying sheep in such a way that he could have provoked the great flock of shepherds? Yet the prophet says: I have nourished and brought up children, and they have despised me. And the Lord says of the apostles: Whoever despises you despises me. The prophet testifies that they were bishops when he says of Judas: And let another take his bishopric. And the apostle Paul likewise proclaims: Obey those set over you, for they will pray for you.

But let us return to that weighty and venerable proposition, which was not only dragged out of a pigsty but positively reeks. "The king's authority," they say, "did not summon all the bishops to the council, nor did all of them agree in the judgment." Slaves of Tartarus and plainly ministers of Satan! Whomever the prince's letter did not summon, the cause has drawn in through new bonds and through the coils of your own deeds. I will not say with what wish and with what intention those men departed who were wearied by the waiting, when they saw that the venerable pope had received a long reprieve in life, against what they considered right. They saw that the darts they had aimed struck only the air. So that these wretches might not be allowed to lurk in secret, consoling themselves for their evil deeds, your books lay bare those who were hidden, and through you they are not allowed solitude in their shameful act, as the Lord says in the Gospels: Everyone who does evil hates the light.

After this you assert that those who accused the aforesaid pope by presenting petitions ought not to have been called adversaries of the Roman pope. To make your claim credible, you add that the royal orders had not called them by that name. O men polished with every file of art and fired in the smiths' furnaces, who have sweated to find testimonies confirming their statements! We love your opinion, reverend sirs, and, as the saying goes, we walk over to it: we acknowledge the errors you speak of. Should anyone call an accuser an enemy, and apply a tragic name to someone who does not deserve the insult? Next you fastened on an appended question with a rhetorical clasp, alleging: "The city of Rome is witness whether all the bishops who assembled were old and feeble." Behold a speech gleaming with the sinews of truth, to be preferred even to Cepasius for the brilliance of its language! So, because they said they were advanced in age and weak in body, they themselves testify, it seems, that they are unfit to judge, since they said they were already suffering the decay of their limbs, especially if they presumed to press this upon the ears of our most clement lord. You, who have been driven from every sight of God, think that things which ought to be reported are confused everywhere, in the manner of your own meetings. You think that before the prince others from the assembly of bishops spoke, and not those whom ripeness of age had made the ones to begin the speech: those on whom their long years conferred reverence, and who were thought to have been preserved so long by the support of their good merits. It was fitting, then, that those whom age had appointed to make the plea should complain of the weariness of heavy age. Excellent men, you added that the reason for the summons was already known from the royal orders, and that the ruler of all Italy ought not to have been consulted as if about some new matter: religion, you say, owed more to paper and writing than to the presence of the prince. So, on your view, no point remained in this business that they might investigate, and so rightly begin with that opening speech! From there you digress to praise the king's love of good things, and with words you cultivate an innocence of which your deeds know nothing — if indeed there is any cultivation in your speech. You plough it up with a rough share, like men driving the plough off the track, entrusting darnel to withered soil, and for such outlay you will reap chaff, with which the fire of Gehenna will be kindled for your destruction.

But now, as someone is reported to have said, what shall I put before what? You say that, contrary to the apostle, the assailants of the supreme pontiff were not heard — they who, mindful of the heavenly command, withdrew their portion from fellowship with an adulterer. Here I do not attack your ignorance, nor do I accuse your leaky memory. I will not say that you have attributed a prophet's words to the apostle, since I know that those too are rightly called apostles whom I know to have been sent. For David says: When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers. Next, who could untangle himself from that question of yours, in which you say: "In charges that are brought, what is not excluded is proven"? Behold a saying fit for the soldiers of the Roman Church, in which you would not know whether to praise first its polish or its flavour! Have you ever, I wonder, heard it read: What is just you shall pursue justly? Have you heard, concerning men's misdeeds — if indeed you have ever lived in human society — that whatever is not proven by proper procedure is excluded? Where is that saying of the prophet: The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people? And what was said of you: They proclaimed their sin like Sodom; woe to their souls! But what is to be done, when no remedy comes to the aid of the desperate, except to implore the Lord, who promised through the prophet that he would come upon everyone proud and lofty and upon everyone arrogant, so that he may be brought low? But I shall follow this foul work step by step, and, if I can, crush it with an iron heel, so that, to speak truly, fact will fight with fact, cause with cause, and reason with what they take for reason. You allege that the bishops spoke against the royal orders, and you think it a kind of sacrilege — since you know nothing of the heavenly Lord — that anything ill should be thought of the command of an earthly lord. You object: "Who had any business telling the king that it was the pope who ought to convoke the synod? What precedent is there on this point? Above all, how could it be he, who already lay prostrate under the criminal charges of many; for whom to be accused was already to be condemned; from whom the denunciations of his enemies had already taken away the prerogative assigned to him from heaven?" Has the growth of your evil deeds dragged you step by step to such madness that you believe accusing is the same as convicting? Are hatreds, in your eyes, no different from the truth — hatreds which mostly contrive, against the merit of the accused, wishes that serve partisanship rather than reason? Where is that saying: Before you understand, do not judge anyone? Long ago the flock placed on the left hand received you as colleagues. Among them, whoever has been brought to examination is believed to have received his sentence by prejudgment, and to enter the scales of debate is to be guilty.

To your preamble, however, you very aptly attached a divine example, so well built of squared-off phrases that you would think Chrysippus himself was holding the line in it: To the sinner God says: Why do you recite my statutes? To this saying you join what amounts to an apostrophe to the bishops: "Because he is reckoned the vicar of blessed Peter the apostle, do you forbid the chief physician to bring medicine to his body? How is it, then, that you refuse to provide a cure for his soul?" By all that is holy, I do not know whether this is a great joke or cause for the deepest lament. You seek a cure for someone else's fever; you want medicine applied to a failing soul; and while you yourselves stand at death's door, you forget yourselves and deliberate about another man's health. What if the prophet truly said this to you: Is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? And again: Physician, heal yourself? But more of this elsewhere. We know that one who has been given up for lost cannot be healed, and that the wicked man, when he comes into the depths, despises everything with astonishing recklessness. But I suppose that counsel still lives in these men even in the death of their evil way of life, and that one can wish for another what he himself has already lost. Now I may rightly say with the prophet: All that this people says is conspiracy; do not fear what it fears, nor be in dread. Away from us with this itching of tongues aimed at us — tongues which the same prophet rightly rebukes: Writing, you have written injustice. We do not hold, as you claim, that blessed Peter, or his successors, received from the Lord, along with the privileges of the see, a license to sin. He handed down to his successors an everlasting dowry of merits together with an inheritance of innocence. What was granted to him for the light of his deeds belongs to those whom a like splendour of life illuminates. For who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up? If goods acquired by merit are lacking in him, those bestowed by the predecessor in that place suffice. For he either raises the illustrious to these heights or makes illustrious those who are raised; for he knows beforehand what is fit for the foundation of the churches, on whom the whole structure rests. But from this you think that heavenly power supports your deeds, because, as you say, you lend a helping right hand to protect the blessed apostle. Do you not know, you fools, that the sun is not helped by torches, nor are lamps lit to support the light of day? For it is written: God searches the hearts and the inmost parts.

But on that point who would dare to answer your arguments, except that truth is spoken without art, while credibility is stitched onto falsehood by verbal tricks? "Why," they say, "did you go to the prince, if the accused was not allowed to be heard?" Does the fog of sin, or divine dread, so bury you in a beast's stupor that your mind either deceitfully passes over a modest excuse or, weighed down by the dullness of brutes, fails to recognize it? Or do you perhaps think that what was said — that he whose office was needed ought himself to convoke the synod — meant anything other than this: that through an episcopal examination the divine sentence should strike you down, whom an insane fervour had cut off from the body of your head, to the ruin of your salvation?

Next you put into your work — whether with words or with barks, I do not know — a mention of Esau, comparing to him your own bishop, as one who lost the benefit of his elder birth by trading it for a single meal, and forfeited the venerable dignity of the firstborn by obeying his gullet. What shall I reply to this, hemmed in as I am on every side by the charges? Which of you, I ask, snatched the blessing from Symmachus by serving his father more devotedly? On which of you was the nobility of such great gifts conferred through the voice of Jacob? Which of you came running to obey the wishes of a blind parent? Which of you, by his devotion, made a venerable father who had lost his sight feel no loss of light? Is it not true that, compared with your darkness, night seems to show a radiance glowing through a clear sky, and every obscurity, compared with your deeds, takes on the beauty of the sun? Moreover, in that case the blessing conferred on Jacob, though it suited the son's character, had nonetheless already been promised. But why do we linger any longer on this, since those who have kicked against the goads cannot be taught? Believe me, what you put forward is hostile to peace and useless for attack.

But next comes a knot with a riddle, and I do not know by what art of rejoinder we may untie it. For they have entered the sea of Ciceronian depth, and with the winds of their questions they drive our little boat among uncertain shores. Yet in that boat, with Christ holding the helm, I shall come into port and deal one by one with all your whirlwinds, having under that guidance a capacity that is not my own. For they say: "If the bishops' assertion is true, that the prelate of the apostolic see has never been subject to the judgment of lesser men, why was he brought to trial by a strict summons?" Here indeed my aged lack of eloquence struggles greatly, and I must call on him who always, together with us, overcomes the weight of a proposition we have not yet grappled with. For I plainly cry out with the prophet on behalf of the bishops: Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him who draws it? And may this divine oracle support me: How the exactor has ceased, and the tribute is at rest! So the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked. Grant, Lord, what you foretold of them: that as a drunkard staggers and vomits, so the unbeliever who acts faithlessly may perish. For this reason the prophet cries out in scorn of you: Hear the word of the Lord, you scoffers. Does anyone fix the outcome of a case on the basis of foreknowledge? When a hasty decision is meant to put an end to raging conflicts, does it measure things in such a way that, once it becomes known to have come before the inquiry, it betrays the favour of the one who judges? Now for a little while, though unworthy in speech, deeds and years, I shall rebuke you with a bishop's voice. We did not wish our statutes to be weighed in the same balance as yours. Canons have been laid down for us concerning the character of accusers, and among us it is a sin to overstep the venerable definitions of the fathers. For us it is written in the Council of Carthage — whose decisions the authority of the apostolic see approved through Bishop Faustinus, who was present then as its envoy — that accusers coming from an enemy's house are not to be believed. In such men a neighbourliness inflamed by hatred stirs up the flame of persecution with dry fuel, and by secret arrangement assembles the whole machinery of deceit, with its expense and its interlocking devices. How could our assembly have known what house had spewed these men out unless they were present? And how could it have learned the nature of the accusation except from a written statement, in which it would recognize the cesspool of crimes, while they pretend that they owe a prosecution to the crimes?

After what was put forward about the accusers, you added the question why the persons whom the imperial authority had often demanded were ordered to be produced, claiming that this served to cheat the spirit of the one who now stands in the apostolic see as in a kind of citadel. Truly Wisdom says to you: A man who is weak and short-lived will not attain understanding; but let him labour to know what is pleasing to the Lord. And again the Proverbs say: He who neglects learning hates himself, for death meets the ignorant. Why do you feign that ignorance which descends from a viper's knowledge? Why do you employ tricks with a brigand's marvellous art, while showing simplicity on your face? Of you it was truly said: Whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own. By crafty foresight you kept from your bishop's eyes the glad face that comes from a court's verdict. You did this so that you might drive him from the very sanctuary of the courts, though he was equipped with such defences against your battle lines and bore the weapons of innocence with the whole world as his witness. You took care that he should neither live, innocent as he was, without being attacked, nor, once assailed, have the comfort of an incorrupt inquiry by judges. You both granted the aforesaid a trial and begrudged it to him, since by one and the same route you both forbid him and force him to face the hazards of debate. By a single path he is summoned to the case only to be barred from it, so that he might neither keep a manifest safety without being attacked nor snatch it by acquittal. I remember reading in the days of my youth a saying about someone: "You order exile for an exile, and do not grant [?]." The prophet's sentence assails you: These are the men who troubled the earth and shook kingdoms. And again: Their shoots will be cut off with pruning hooks, and what is left will be cut away. And again: When you do not expect it, your ruin will come, and your multitude will be broken like a potter's jar. The prophet also thundered, speaking expressly to this case: The Lord will stretch out his hand, and he who brings help to the wicked will fall, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all be consumed together. But after these ancient refuges of examples I return to the newer definitions of the canons. The Council of Carthage cries out in another place: Whatever persons the public laws do not admit to make an accusation, we too deny them leave to attack another. I ask you, men endowed with a perfection polished to the fingernail: what was the status of those slaves whom you reported as demanded in the prince's letters? If a servile chain still held them in another's power, and no step taken into freedom had loosed them from the fetters of their base bondage, would the words of these persons have carried any credibility even with you as judges? But, I suppose, you will reply that the truth, which their voluntary statements could hardly fail to lack, would have been extracted from its hiding places by a devout torturer using various torments, so that, while their bodies were broken by punishments, their souls would not conceal what they knew had been done. But I beg you, turn your faces first to the public laws, and then to the judges, who can speak thus in their own defence: "We have been made free by the service of God after casting off such things. We either despise or laugh at the insults of jeering slaves. To us the apostle wrote concerning servants: Remember that both their Lord and yours is in heaven. Shall we be called back to these evils of the world? Must we do what we maintain makes anyone else who does it profane? Shall a thing which would defile our sight even if carried out through the ministry of an order and by another's hands be accomplished at our command?" Do not keep this attitude toward all the churches, after the manner and nature of ravening wolves. For even after a bloody interrogation had perhaps stained us as you desire, it would not have achieved in them the result you are aiming at. But, as the prophet tells us, let us put a ring in your nose and a bridle in your lips, and lead you back by the way you came. You are under attack, as the same prophet declares when he says: They shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose you shall perish.

You have also added this new invention against us: that our Lord and Redeemer himself submitted to the judgment of servants, and that the Maker of heaven willingly placed himself beneath a mere particle of earth, when he testifies and says: "Man of Judah, and you who dwell in Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard." You relate that blessed Peter and the apostle Paul did not shrink from this either. You drag that fine eloquence of yours into the argument from law, leading the way with chains of precedents, as though you still had a contest here with a resisting opponent, and what is freely offered had to be wrung out by the strong fingers of your eloquence. You say that even the wonderful prophet Samuel appealed to the testimony of the people about the clearness of his conscience. But what did Samuel say? That the Lord knew he had never carried off anyone's property or anyone's livestock, that he had set himself against bribes and, what is beyond human strength, had shunned even gifts that came unasked. He was taking care, of course, that his reputation should not suffer harm through the prejudgments of suspicion. In the end he made his innocence plain under divine witness, precisely so as not to undergo a human examination. As for our Redeemer, when he wishes a judgment to take place between himself and his vineyard, he is rather calling for judgment, looking at wrongs like yours in the present affair. Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, when he was accused through the malice of your fellows, recognized that the multitude of insults brought him exercise, not fear. Truly he added to the value of his crown whatever he gave up of his dignity, and before the heavenly sentence of acquittal, as a good judge of innocence, he played the part of a defendant. For this is how the soldiers of Christ bring forth by their own sweat an increase of honor for themselves: they chasten the heights granted them with a loftier humility, and so purchase heaps of praise from the very fact that they govern the summits they have attained with sublime restraint. And although his see shows blessed Athanasius, so far as one may know, to be unequal to the Roman pontiff, the two are comparable in how they acted in their affairs. The one presented himself to his judges; the other, as even you say, summoned his. The one, as a servant of God, did not flee the inquiry brought against him; the other placed the hope of his triumph in the assembling of examiners. But why linger longer on these comparisons? This man too wanted judgment, loved it, drew it on, and entered upon it; and, a thing that could rouse the hearts of the faithful with the stings of just grief, he granted the venerable council authority even against himself, should he deserve it. Seeing this face of his own plea, who would not know that he came to his fellow bishops supported by the testimony of his purity? What he dreaded was that their strict judgment should have too little authority, for he reckoned that whatever a judge without authority decided would be all the more easily overthrown in one way or another. Why do you assail him with doglike chatter? Why do you wound one who does not deserve it? What you think is your threat is his wish. But the venom of the new serpent hisses more cunningly in you than in the adversaries of Athanasius. They did not know what you know very well: how to take a triumph away from the accused. They were afraid that the man they had challenged would not appear to be heard; you, unable to bear the delay that the hearings involved, drove him back with missiles as he came, and in place of the vexation the sentence had in store for you, you took up avenging arms. O recollection of evils, which both supplies the voice and undermines it, since by the very weight of the deeds it confounds the words of those it has driven to cry out!

Who could bear your chattering calmly? So, according to your claim, we do not love the benefits of new advantage because we show obedience to what our elders decreed? Here you hoist all the sails of your wit; here, with neck thrown back, a belch has vomited up from the recesses of the breast whatever wind it had. For they say: "If you follow only what is old, you condemn the fasts of Moses and the miracles Elisha performed when he raised the dead." What reasoning can a competent investigator find here? Not even a pale prospector for gold, should he come along, would find in your thoughts the course of hidden veins, or, digging among your words, let light into such unaccustomed hiding places. Do we then reject hoary miracles because we refuse our consent to youthful excesses? If, mindful of the Gospel, we subject servant to master and disciple to teacher, are we neglecting whatever could be of profit? There are other things, most shameless of men, that we put to present use without injury to antiquity.

Next you have opened up a new charge, one our inquiry had passed over: "Why did the pope, with no precedent established before him, convoke a synod to examine the charges brought against him?" After this you accuse us of falsehood because we say that the letters written in this affair were requested from the king. Grant, Lord, that we may pass through the winding turns of this labyrinth without straying. Make straight the path that the supple serpent traces according to the shape of its own body or mind, so that we may truly say: "The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper," and rejoice with Solomon, who says: "The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but all protection is with the Lord." It is indeed superfluous to answer absurd propositions, since the prophet says: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly." But if contempt passes over anything, I fear it may be thought that fear kept us from touching it, as though it were strong. It is better for us, with blessed Paul, to cut away the grounds for mockery and testify with full voice: "I have become a fool; you compelled me." Was there then no precedent for the pope to convoke a council of bishops, when it is his decision to assemble a synod? Or were those crimes of yours that this great assembly was to condemn mere trifles? Are not the words of the canons direct: that any cleric who departs from his bishop on a doubtful suspicion before the time of sentence remains under manifest censure? For the service of this matter a company devoted to God had to gather, so that an army of physicians might relieve the sores of a lost and ruined flock. For whenever the violence of disease hastens with swift step to the hidden places of the soul, saving counsel cannot bring its hands to meet it except by the consultation of many. Indeed our petition asked this too of the king: that, with the prejudgments of the clergy cut away, heavenly authority should judge through human mouths the deserts of the pope's accusers. But let us look, if you please, and reread those subtleties of your instructive pamphlet, keeping before our eyes the decrees of the fathers, by which the bilge of your excesses may be weighed. Church law requires that a bishop accused by others not be abandoned before the charges have been established in the light of day. But you, mindful, I suppose, of divine law, who despise light errors and delight in the nobility of sin, did not want only one fault, the desertion of your bishop, to be laid at your door, and so you accused him as well, adding to your offenses. He who is your leader brought you to such strength that, after abandoning the pontiff and attacking him, you believed that the judgment of the bishops of almost all Italy should be rejected without the force of any sentence. As someone said of a company like yours: "He did not entrust his hastening soul to a single death." Can you, unteachable mind, now enriched by the successes of your crimes, ever rest from your detestable purpose, as though worn out? He made you rich in these evils whom an abundance of pride robbed of angelic wealth, and whose overflowing treasury of harm made him begrudge the divine estate.

But, mindful of our promise, let us touch on everything we recall being included in their work. In a most splendid style Pope Symmachus is charged with having come to the hearing ahead of the summons, with crowds of people, and afterward with having scorned the judgment, though summoned four times. Has love of truth so deserted you that you think the testimony of the whole world can be wrapped in clouds of lies, and that words painted with the brush of deceit have more force than the truth that Rome holds? Did he then approach the hearing unseasonably, or flee it when he was awaited? Was it not Christian expectation, born of zeal for the faith, rather than fury, that called out that multitude of people devoted to God? Does anyone who runs to commit violence take tears as his companions? Does one who sets out to inspire terror show the face of one afraid? That multitude, attending the bishop in his office, brought us laments, not missiles. It came not menacing with weapons but pitiable with weeping, and it was to weigh against your charge by one display alone: with rich rivers from its eyes it showed how grievous, through your bitterness, was the plight of the man under attack, and, in the sobriety of a venerable hearing, it commended by its own distress the one it could not commend by voice. But this makes plain what fury kindles your bile: that a man for whom the world weeps came to judgment all but acquitted. And while in your speech you heap up against him an odium foreign to the facts, your long-proud neck bows for a little while to our reverence. For you call it a sacred assembly only when you want to claim that Symmachus is our destroyer, and with cruel piety you think that whatever he lost while sitting in the citadel of the churches accrues to our honor. Not only did we not feel any of this; we feel the opposite. Turn the poisons of your protection toward others instead. He who spends the service of his tongue on someone who resists it has no standing as a defender; he who confers something on an unwilling person loses what he imagines to be the gratitude owed for a favor, for nothing is a gift unless you wish to receive it.

Now there is no need of long admonition for those already lost. We owe our hatred to a work whose authors have nothing left in them still to be condemned. With urbane coloring you assert that crowds of women came to the hearing with him, and by that subtlety of yours you single out the sex that, you imply, had more affection for the bishop than it should. Most profane of men, I hold fast to what is written: it is one thing to speak evil, another to accuse; and to what the prophet said: "Rejecting the word, you have put your hope in slander and in tumult, and you rest in it; therefore this iniquity shall be to us like a breach." For God says on our behalf: "But those who judge you, I will judge." And again he says to his servants: "Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies." And once more he cries out to you: "Come here, you offspring of the adulterer and the fornicator! Whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened wide your mouth and stuck out your tongue? Are you not wicked children, a lying brood?"

Notice what you join to what when you say: "The pope departed with his case unpleaded, abandoning his advocates," setting before us in the present affair examples from the forum and the streets, whose hypocrites you are. For us it is written through the apostle Paul of those to whom the world is crucified: what have they to do with the forum? But you do not know these things, or, what is worse, you know them and despise them. I suppose the pope departed because he was demanding something strange and divorced from reason! Did he not, bound by pastoral care for the state of a tottering church, hope for exactly what both religious foresight and the order of the case itself demanded? For what form of trial had gone before? We had been torn apart in hostile fashion, and the church's wealth had been taken away, even at your instigation, so that he who had long been food for the hungry was seen to have become the slave of famine, since the distributor himself lacked nourishment, and there was servitude in lordship and lordship in servitude. What precedent of a former age, handed down in memory for all to see, warranted this? What could a man become by being convicted by a verdict, when in his case judgment came before trial? There was no privilege left of which one already stripped bare could be despoiled. You thought that one resource remained to you in the sacred assembly: to join bishops to yourselves as companions in defending the enormity of your crimes, so that the deed might go unpunished through the defilement of many. A judge is never brought in at the proper time when he is summoned to a case all but decided. Even if the accused deserves it, the accuser takes that away when he wants his own fury to have more license against him than the judge has. For the prophet says, attacking you: "This is the portion of those who laid us waste, and the lot of those who plundered us. Go, swift angels, to a flock torn and mangled, to a terrible people." An angel has been sent to you, namely through the bishops, by whose voice and merit gifts are received to be carried to Christ, and who, once the Lord is appeased, bestow on mortals the prayers they have obtained. Through them the gifts of concord were offered to you, gifts you rejected. They offered the rewards of love to those who deserved punishment, and, considering what befitted themselves, they paid no regard at all to what you deserved.

"Who," they say, "saw him clash with his accusers in what they call open battle?" Most shameless of men, consider whom you want to contend with whom, and, if any soundness is left in you, attend to the places, times and persons on both sides. And if the wickedly amassed wealth of your depraved heart has not yet subdued you, lift your eyes to God for a little while, and for even a short time scorn the commands of your sinister counselor. You recognize that in these matters, which deserve punishment, you are not protected by the commands of the sovereign king. For although the terms of a request dictate the character of the reply, and a petition, by going first, sketches out what is to follow, you have never caught the free words of the ruler in your nets; never have imperial letters served your desires through your cunning fowling. How often has the ineffective bite of malice snapped shut on empty air? How often has whatever you held in hope against the accused slipped away, and the phantom seized by presumption left you empty-handed? Thanks be to God, who has implanted this foresight in the one to whom he entrusted the sum of human affairs. Perfect wisdom in the helmsman is a sure hope of peace and safety. A ship whose master is fitted by the gift of understanding to steer at the helm has everywhere an anchorage, everywhere a harbor amid the waves. The security of all is certain when the state is governed by one trained in noble arts. The heaven-inspired governance of our emperor knows how to put out a hand to block wits notorious for deceit. No effort is needed with him, for naked truth long ago received him as its defender. Let the wicked cease to feign with fraud a fabricated simplicity before him: whatever stirs against justice is soon caught. With him nothing is safer than innocence. He who sets before him matters in keeping with equity has a strong embassy. The assault that so often weighs on princes, the flattery of the less loyal, finds no hearing [?] with him. But these things are better told to God, from whom the plant of this fruit comes.

The unwelcome nature of the task I have undertaken brings me back to you, though until now I have wished to devote my effort to better discourse; but imperious necessity demands a speech held captive. For you said: "How were you deliberating at first about the case or its nature, when the synod did not yet have validity?" O the effrontery of foul speech, and the face of a pamphlet stained by more than ignorance alone! You both describe the scope of our deliberation and question it. This, of course, is exactly what we were in doubt about, because, as you say, the synod did not have validity: the nature of the affair was beyond those who were to hear it, and more still remained in our reverence for the man accused than lay in the integrity of our college.

Then, in connection with the interrogations under torture, you reply that the venerable bishops Laurence and Peter suspended themselves from communion with the pope, and you turn whatever the caution of those convened provided for into a charge against the accused. Was there then ever a time, when they celebrated the sacred rites of the Mass, that the commemoration of his name ceased? Did the bishops you name ever, as you would wish, offer half-complete sacrifices, without the Catholic rite and ancient custom? Was there ever, so that it might be laid to your account, an offense against God committed through grace, and did the offering, nurse of pardon, become the mother of sin? Those you speak of were indeed separated only by not gathering together in body; they did not shun the presence of souls. If you think that men are cut off from mutual fellowship when the clasp of religion, biting with its holy tooth, holds them together, your bias has led you far from a sound judgment of faults. It is dwelling in the heavenly commandment that unites or separates us. It makes no difference what distances divide us if we are held in one chamber in the mansion above. Truly we infer from this that you are slaves of the belly and the body, and by the cheapness of this opinion you declare yourselves earthly chattels. For it is written: "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit."

After this, with your ranks turned to flight, you added in the manner of frenzied speech: "So then, have the councils of bishops held every year throughout the provinces, as church law decrees, lost their force because the pope is not present at them?" Read, you utter madmen, if you can find that anything was ever decided in them without the sanction of the apostolic eminence, or that any weightier matter that came up for discussion was not reserved to the judgment of that see. For this is what you have: "If any bishop has been deposed by a provincial judgment, let him, if he wishes, appeal again to the Roman pope, and let the pope, if he sees fit, renew the trial in aid of the condemned man." See, the snare you prepared is untied, unless perhaps we are bound in that quarter by the tightest of knots and the paths of reply are closed to us, a path once open being now overgrown with thickets by some new obstruction.

For with these brambles of eloquence you hold us back as we walk on level ground, when you say that the king was offended because we wanted the visitor assigned against church rules to withdraw at the very outset. We wanted this so that vice should have no further license then, so that the tares should not harden, so that the profane crop should not go uncut by the sickle of discipline before it ripened, and so that what the judges did not forbid should not be thought permitted. From this it is plain that you are supported by no authority of precedent apart from the eminence of the most pious king, which you vainly wish to link with wrongdoing. It remains for me to show that he too, by good fortune for all, is not implicated in these excesses. For he wished the man he sent to be not an occasion of strife or the kindling of a quarrel, but a cause of concord. He foresaw, of course, that unless he fenced that simple man about with the protection of his orders, your poisons would soon snatch him away to be fodder for discord. For it is written: "The simple man believes every word." Therefore he fixed a boundary to his mandate that no transgression might violate. He commanded him, as soon as he had been brought to Rome, to go to the basilica of blessed Peter, thus making the bishop's wish a king's command. For who would not have thought that the pontiff would willingly comply in a matter that the king did not believe even himself permitted to forbid? And there he ordered that, after greeting the pope, the visitor should tell him in the king's own words to hand over to his fellow bishop the slaves, who were to be subjected to no torture but kept, certainly, for the hearing of the synodal inquiry. O purity of the command, which, while it carries a torch before the present age, drives antiquity into shadow, and snatches the light from the old with the unprecedented splendor of novelty! What man rich in words, what fabricator of reputation, ever attached such a thing to anyone poor in merit? Who ever enriched with invented praises the fame of a lord whose deeds in truth left him a beggar? I do not disparage before you the writers through whose kindness the deeds of our ancestors have come down to us adorned. But I will not keep silent about the gifts of God, for our prince surpasses in deeds the ornaments of words. He does not seek glory that depends on tongues; whatever is added to his praise he considers idle. Consider with what careful balance, as on a scale, the venerable weigher of cases examined the matter, so that, while skillfully granting your petition its effect, he nevertheless preserved church law in everything. What hearts, however much sharper than others, are equal to such judgment? At one time, by one writing, your wishes are fulfilled without harm to equity, and the same document is directed both to the service of religion and to your joy. For the good prince in his inquiry foresaw that the assertion of slaves was not to be put to proof in the trial of an innocent man. In choosing the venerable judges he himself set aside the accusers as irregular, and he himself restored the accused to hope.

Let us see, however, whether these things were done, and whether you were not enemies both of God and of your earthly lord, since you despise Christ and the king with equal rashness, and one chain of crimes has led you to insult both. The bishop who had been sent was snatched away by the coils of your speech at the very point of carrying out his commission. He had come to serve as a soldier of peace, and he was turned into a means of stirring up confusion. Without visiting the threshold of the blessed apostle, he was summoned to serve your fury, no longer himself. That foundation of the churches, which draws the devout from every corner of the world, lay close by and was passed over: he was not allowed to approach so modest a structure [?]. Then, cut off from the root, he lost the hope of good fruit. You may perhaps say that it detracts from the apostle's dignity to suppose that a citizen of heaven is confined to places on earth. Yet although blessing is granted everywhere to those who ask, and the faith and devotion of the suppliant claim the martyr's presence, it cannot be denied that more is granted to devotion at the place of his heavenly birth, and that the places from which saints pass to the heights win greater affection. The multitude of cures has already lent credibility to this claim, and we can call as witnesses those already healed after being besieged by the devil. Although such things are celebrated throughout the world through our Redeemer, that tomb has gained no small renown from the crowds that visit it, because through him who changed man into an angel the very nature of earth could be made glorious. You begrudged your visitor this grace, thinking that he would stop following your errors if he had touched the inner sanctuary of that revered passion. See, you have no support in royal authority. See, after heaven's displeasure, the censure of the prince, whom you caused to be spurned, justly strikes you as well.

Let us see whether any defense remains in the argument from the rules. “He himself,” they say, “gave visitors to other bishops as well, and it is just that he should be bound by the law of his own act.” I do not attack you here for the falsehood of this claim. I do not refute words long attached to lies. But I say this: the maker of a law is not confined within the limits of his own definition unless he wishes to be, and unless the sovereign tempers the height of his supremacy of his own accord [?], it is in vain that he is summoned to the law he himself gave. There is a law of uprightness and of the mind that disciplines a man who lives without law: whoever does not owe discipline to necessity rightly devotes it to good conduct. Perhaps God willed that the cases of other men be settled by men, but he reserved the bishop of this see, beyond question, to his own judgment. He willed that the successors of the blessed apostle Peter should owe their innocence to heaven alone, and present an untouched conscience to the scrutiny of the most searching of examiners. Do not suppose that the souls which God has reserved above all others for his own examination have no fear of their examiner. Before him the accused finds no help in the polish of his pleading, since the one who witnesses his deeds is the one who judges them. You may perhaps say: “Such will be the condition of all souls at that trial.” I will reply that it was said to one man: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven also.” And again, that through the voice of holy bishops the dignity of his see has been made venerable throughout the world, since all the faithful everywhere are subject to it, since it is designated head of the whole body. Of it, I think, the prophet said: “If this is humbled, to whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory?”

What if I, though my lips are unclean and have not been washed in the fire of a burning coal as was granted to Isaiah, were allowed to call upon the apostle Peter himself to defend the privileges of his possession, and he were to speak in a human voice what he does through his prayers? If you heard him, this is what he would say: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful. Why do you long to undermine the foundations laid by the hands of Christ? Why do you batter with a ram the [?] of the possession of him who is renewed through faults [?], and by tearing apart the church's flock subject me to fresh sufferings even after the flesh? It is an unheard-of kind of sacrilege that you dress up in the honor of a counterfeit religion. A man dishonors the reverence due to a venerable name when he offers himself as its helper in matters he claims were committed against God. It is a kind of insult to pose as coming to the aid of the Most High, as the apostle says: ‘Who are you to judge another's servant?’ Why do you make sport of untrained ears and make the show of vengeance more serious than the fault? If you owe hatred to wrongdoing, cleanse yourselves. Why are you freer to condemn crimes than to avoid them? A man attacks himself when he presses charges of adultery by means of fornication and accuses the flesh through the defilement of souls. Surely you remember what is written: ‘Cursed are all who go whoring away from you.’ So whoever renders his duties to the heavenly statutes with less than pure faith is cut off by a foul bond from the splendor of his Lord. The brilliance of our possession, as I see, has stirred your envy, and you disguise it as indignation at the possessor's faults while you toil and spend. The citadel that made you conspicuous you set out to undermine, shaking it with blow after blow, and had I not resisted you would have shown by its ruin how great a structure heaven had established. Do not look for victory from your own disaster. Do not lose, by conquering, a triumph won by my labors and my sweat. Whatever leads to a trophy, I have won. Whatever would make you illustrious, I have gathered into this see. That torch, which you think can be put out with viper's venom, is what gives you your brightness. Whoever so rages against the shoots of his own grace that he cuts down the plants is kindled to his own destruction: anger more unrestrained than is just harms its author more than anyone else.

“As for what you call the excesses of Symmachus, if they exist, I bear with them in the same patient expectation with which I bear with you. It is wicked for a sinner not to love the patience of a judge. What is a man demanding but vengeance, when, guilty himself, he complains that punishment is delayed for another? I owe these words to such zeal, because I hold that God said that man is prone to wickedness and that all flesh is friendly to sin. I do not want the possession that is to give dignity to countless people to be brought low on account of one person, lest the divine law be broken while a man is attacked. Believe me, if the things you allege are true, I am attending to them, for I have examined what was the case even with those of whom nothing of the kind was said. He is wrong who thinks that one who stands next to God can be deceived: ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.’ Instead, you who were once my sons, with whom the womb of spiritual birth was heavy, return to the concord you have forsworn. Let mother church receive you into her loving bosom, as she has held you until now. Correction is never too late. She knows how to wait long for those she has sought with immense labor; she does not know how to despise as worthless those bought at a great price. There are many steps by which to return to salvation; no one is shut out except the one who despairs; the fruit of pardon comes next after the crown. Do not help Pope Symmachus by pressing upon him: if he is guilty, believe me, once the service of human attack has ceased, divine judgment will soon follow. Is not either punishment or reward owed to him in the scales of the most glorious Judge? Do not look to me for syllogisms and figures of speech. I still use the old net to fish for men, and I have not abandoned the little boat that the wise of this world laugh at. It carries me through the straits of the world; the net you see, proven in catching men, makes me rich.”

“Come back, then, since your flight has not yet carried you off to become wild. Run to the fold, so that you do not expose yourselves to the snares of wolves, and do not by delay lose the grace given to those who come of their own accord, for hell follows an invitation that is scorned. If I have shown any of the gentleness I owed you as a father, if I have exercised any of the strictness due from a teacher appointed by God, see to it that a sparse crown of Levites does not much longer surround my cross, whatever corner of it remains, that a desolation grievous even to strangers does not reign for long, and that the labor of my womb does not prove to have borne, in place of barrenness, a hostile household, so that a numerous offspring by its wicked deeds shows the mother to be infertile. Few are the things I have said, but consider how much hangs on them. Come, sons, listen to me: I have taught you the fear of the Lord. Look at Rome. The shedding of Christ's blood set her free from slavery to idols at no price of gold or silver, and he ordered that my death too, the death of his humble servant, be spent for her. For many ages she offered worship in famous temples; for long she revered in the images of demons the terror that the master craftsman's hand had put into them at great cost; she looked up to the power of deities bought at the price of metal; a more practiced craftsman's hand produced loftier gods for her, and the divinity that man conferred by his handiwork had greater standing among men than God. See, now by Christ's favor the idols have gone back to new furnaces. See, now your daily use draws something to rejoice in from that outworn superstition, as new little vessels are rightly made from the old Thunderer. Why do you strive to break this peace? Why make sport of this happiness with empty schemes? This fury has no excuse, believe me. It makes no difference by what road a man runs to the prince of this world once he has broken away from holy unity: whoever saddens the church offers fat victims to the devil. Reject, then, these empty snares. The love of peace has a simple defense. He is armed enough who scorns the weapons the adversary supplies against concord. The bare opposition of faith is enough against all the darts of quarreling. Why, in search of comfort for your evils, do you drag up the times of Eulalius and Boniface? Why do you bring forward old contagions to increase present excesses, and out of malice refuse to let the passage of time cover old offenses? The cause of discord was different then, and if recounting it would not force me to live through the past again, I would show you that no comfort comes from comparing the two cases. Those two whom the zeal of faction had raised to the pontifical summit I rejected, both of them, and I chose this one, for, as the outcome testifies, neither of them pleased me. Of these present two, I made a fugitive of the one who strove against the rules, and I preserved the one lawfully promoted, though the world attacked him. You know this, and it is nothing new, for when the one was driven out and the other confirmed, your own assent served my cause.”

“Then why, to your own ruin, do you wound the council of bishops? Why do you tear apart the sentence in which, by Christ's inspiration, heavenly oracles were revealed, and the tongue of the bishops stood as interpreter between God and men? Why do you make a wrong committed against one church, the chief one indeed, but one, into the grief of the universal church? That heavenly court, enriched with the gifts of its various seats of honor and adorned with the abundant gold and purple of our Redeemer, put forth nothing in that decision on its own authority, but through the ministry of human tongues it served the divine command. It understood that whatever it decreed under that prompting was not its own. It has nothing in that sentence except what it may rejoice in for its devotion alone. Its pen felt an eloquence not its own, and took from it only this glory: that it kept and honored what was poured into it. Why have you built up a slander against these men out of examples from the Gospels? As is written of you: ‘They erred through drunkenness, they did not know the seer, they were ignorant of judgment.’ For when you cut down the men I have mentioned with profane words, you betray both your ignorance and your envy. So these men do not believe in the resurrection of the body that they preach, and have mixed themselves with the contagion of heretics? They follow in their hearts what they renounce with their tongues? So because they said that he is to be feared who can kill the body and cast the soul into hell, they have woven something foreign to the faith? What profound ignorance! Look at blessed Luke, whose statement can refute you, for he cries: ‘Fear him who, after he has killed the body, has power to cast the soul into hell.’ What room for error is there here, where the words of the saying and of the narrative agree and run along the same line, and what is put forward does not differ from catholic understanding or from the readings? It is never right to look for a knot in a bulrush. Clouds do not wrap round those who preach the author of light. So they do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh because they confess that the body can be killed and that the sinful soul is handed over to hell? Your heart is choked with thick brambles and strives to ascribe its own inner vices to others. You also make much of the claim that the writings of the apostle John were tampered with, because it was said in his words: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth is not in us.’ I make no complaint about the differences between manuscripts. So were the apostle's warnings corrupted because they did not add ‘we deceive ourselves,’ and added ‘we are liars,’ as though they knew nothing not only of divine but even of human reasoning? Whoever does not have the truth is rightly judged a liar, and whoever is known to be empty of integrity is full of nothing but falsehood. But these wounds in us are not to be healed by the speech of the tongue but by groans [?], and it is tears rather than words that should be offered to you, for plainly he is guilty who lays against the innocent either the deserts or the name of the guilty.”

“I will not go back over the remaining heads of your charges: things that deserve condemnation are better buried in silence. Whoever hands on the airing of crimes to the ears of posterity by repeating them over and over gives them renown. We must follow the counsel of blessed Paul, who through his disciple warns everyone and cries: ‘Avoid foolish questions.’ For there is much in your arguments that the love of sin embraces with such filthy arms that it becomes unworthy of mention. Still more is disgraced by levity, since your words are gutted, their weight withdrawn, and windy talk is composed about matters of religion. It has the gravity that suits the ear, but amid its abundance of chaff it will bring no wheat into the barns; it brings forth a lush growth of stalks that bear no grain, and cheats the farmers with the hope held out by the luxuriant grass. Whatever the winnowing fans find no profit in is owed to the fire and will perish in the flames. Of such it is written: ‘They have slept their sleep, and found nothing.’ Nothing, dearest ones, is sweeter than peace, provided a heart full of bitterness does not shut out its taste. I ought indeed to have given a shorter admonition, but no small concern for you, and your faces long hardened by quarrels, drew it out to this length. It is usual that those who sin much are not corrected by a brief address, and they require in the words of the one who admonishes them the same expansiveness they indulged in their offenses. It is enough for me to have answered your diligence and obeyed heaven's commands. In what follows I will leave no room for speeches, for this is what I report: that Rome, the head of the world, has been laid low by your schemes, and that the chair which nurtures the pontificate is looked down on as though it were the lowest seat.”

Blessed Paul took up where he left off, and thundered with the freedom of speech he always used. He rebuked the prince of the apostles for his mildness, because he still kept a parent's affection for minds dissolute and abandoned, and did not bring the healing knife to ulcers that had spread deep. Paul taught that the hidden seats of disease must be cut open with the blade and that a saving wound must be applied when the case is plainly desperate, lest, while the physician's hand is held back by mistaken pity from cutting the corrupt flesh, death be invited by withholding the knife. For when the right hand spares the sick, it kills those it ought to cure, and there is little difference between causing death and allowing it. Whoever could keep death from the sick and does not has inflicted it. With these words, then, he opened the door of his mouth against them:

“Whoever you are who judge, in judging another you condemn yourself, for you who judge do the same things. But we know that the judgment of God falls according to truth on those who do such things. And again: ‘Blessed is he who does not condemn himself in what he approves.’ What perverse reasoning is it that a thief should preach against stealing, and cover a brow that has squandered its shame with the cloud of attacking others? No one rightly takes on the role of admonisher unless he condemns wrongdoing by his own actions and shows his love of innocence by his way of life. For even publicans can condemn in words the vices that are dear to their habits, and punish what they love by the still more wicked services of the tongue, as if it were not a kind of greater excess to lend your lips to a cause you despise in your mind, and to clothe the poison of your heart in the honey of speech. I speak this way as though you had any shame, modesty, grace or affection, or as though anyone were permitted to accuse his teacher and to sink the bites of a spiteful mouth into one of the elect, when I, foreseeing the future, had warned you plainly in the letter I sent you: ‘Who will bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is there to condemn?’ And again: ‘O man, you who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, do you suppose you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience and long-suffering?’ You accuse others of malice, while you yourselves are filled with iniquity, fornication, avarice, wickedness, envy, murder, condemnation, deceit and malignity; proud, haughty, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy. You teach that no one should associate with fornicators, you who are either the followers or the forerunners of the adulterous Laurentius, through whom he either put forth the poisons he had or received those he displayed by pouring them out. After that stain of seductive communion, a plague cursed by the whole world, you blame the priests of God as though they had been joined to a defiled communion [?]. You think those guilty who entered into fellowship with a man convicted by no witness, and you follow a man run through by the whole ecclesiastical indictment—I will not say by its pen, but by its sword. What is lawful is unlawful, and what is unlawful is lawful. As Jannes and Jambres opposed the truth, so do you: corrupt in mind, traitors to the faith, reckless, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, holding the form of godliness but denying its power. O the force of inner grief! It cannot bring forth what it has conceived, and it breaks off the urge to speak that it had itself planted deep in the heart. I will say nothing more to you: lamentations will supply what remains of my speech.”

After this, if under the physicians' hands you grow sicker from the treatment, and no thought of salvation turns you back from your undertaking, at least look to your city, the parent of the world. After her defenders the apostles, she herself comes to you grieving, she herself addresses you, and, if any piety is left in you, she begins a speech that will win its plea:

“Look at me. The temples of the most high God have made me conspicuous, turning away from the worship of shrines and rejoicing in the brilliance of a new light. After filthy sanctuaries polluted with the gore of countless beasts, the outpouring of the blood of the Lord and of the apostles cleansed me of the blood of victims. Health restored after long fevers taught me to despise the temples. The one Offering freed me from sacrifices. I gained the peace of Christ through enmity with idols. I once had scarcely more gifts than gods; my religion made me a beggar through its many devotions; want had crushed me as I constantly begged favors from my gods. I sent the Curii, the Torquati, the Camilli, whom the church did not give new birth, and all the rest down to Tartarus—a barren mother of very many children—while I withered, my womb exhausted by its ill-fated fruitfulness. For saving their country did not redeem the Fabii, and glory won by much toil availed the Decii nothing. Innocence of works without faith was brought to ruin: Scipio, most scrupulous in justice, was ranked among criminals because he did not know Christ. I would gladly run my pen through the whole of my infancy, if the heart of a bereaved mother allowed it. But whoever rereads past lamentations seems to wish for times of weeping. No one is believed to have loved those whose story does not wound him to tell; a man who keeps a dry face while recounting the funerals of his children is convicted of cruelty by a sure witness. That offspring brought more grief in being lost than joy in being gained. Let us recount, however, the happy turns by which all this has been changed. See, now in that sanctuary of liberty nothing servile is found of the worship of idols. See, the crown of honors, the genius of the world, the flower of Rome, the order long revered, now in full holiness tramples on the altars. See, my senate is now called to heaven, praised and received, and I cannot say that I have lost a single child after the grace of baptism, not even one whom sudden death carried off. The supreme Ruler embraces many who hold the robe of state and the curule chair, without loss of worship or of dignity; the munificence of an earthly triumph now almost purchases divine favor, and it profits the grace of Christ that you, my venerable sons, devote yourselves to the world. I lie if needy crowds do not await the coming of your consulship for relief of their misery. Indeed your purple, by which you ennoble the name of the year, drives away with generous gifts of clothing the cold that creeps upon the wretched. Once again the honors of the consular rolls almost bring help to the needy, and now that the old unbelief has been laid aside, through such provision the outlay of wealth becomes gain for souls. See, now the thresholds of the apostle's confession, wet with tears, send candidates to the chair of state, and with abundant tears drawn out by joy the gifts bestowed by God's kindness are doubled.”

"At a time when we drain our breasts for precious offspring, when the eternal mother now takes up our children to bear them a second time, whose womb after their first birth is filled with aged offspring, who by giving them new birth makes sweet to me the children I bore, who makes those who come [?] to her put off old age and makes the broken return to the beginnings of life: who, I ask, would trade this happiness for accusations? Who, through discord sown by a viper's mind, would order the blessings of my golden age to perish? Who secretly breathes ruin into my renewal, and under the guise of a smiling face gathers strength for hostility? I do not recognize noble lineage in such an affair. If, however, there are any of the highest rank whom the storm of this tempest has thrown together with base men, they are stained by sharing in crimes of which others are the authors. Brilliance of blood, even if it falls into partnership in crime, still does not know how to make itself the leader of wrongdoers. It may perhaps bear guilt for neglecting caution; it does not deserve the punishment due to those who lead in crime. A man who is drawn into quarrels already full-grown joins the offenders with a certain shame; he does not deserve to be despaired of as lost, when all that is censured in him is too ready a credulity. It is rather you I see, you spawn of the crossroads, you I recognize, in whom a base nature has produced manners to match it, for whom to have fallen below your birth would have been a distinction, who under the cloak of a feigned religion delight in impunity for your vices, whose lips have never touched the taste either of honours or of peace, who violate every right by obeying your origins, whom the present affair has dragged out of hiding places and caves and put on display. Before this evil was contrived, who knew what you were? For a long time you kept to the obscurity in which the night of your birth had hidden you. Go back, rather, to the blindness you love; leave to us the clear light of day; give the Church concord, either by your absence or by your amendment. If, however, you wish to be counted among illustrious lineages, I shall recognize it by the reform of your conduct."
